title: Thermodynamics
description: Thermodynamics — Class 11 Physics (NCERT): zeroth & first law, internal energy, heat and work, isothermal/adiabatic/isobaric/isochoric processes, second law, Carnot engine & refrigerators with solved numericals & tests.

topics.title: Thermal Equilibrium & the First Law
topics.concept:
Thermodynamics is the branch of physics that deals with heat, work and the conversion of one into the other. Unlike kinetic theory, which looks at individual molecules, thermodynamics describes a system using a few large-scale measurable quantities. A thermodynamic system is the definite quantity of matter (often a gas) chosen for study; everything outside it is the surroundings, and the two are separated by a real or imaginary boundary.

The state of a system is fixed by its state variables — pressure $P$, volume $V$, temperature $T$ and amount of substance $n$. These describe the condition of the gas, not how it got there. For an ideal gas they are linked by the equation of state $PV=nRT$.

  • Thermal equilibrium: two systems in contact are in thermal equilibrium when there is no net flow of heat between them, i.e. they are at the same temperature.
  • Zeroth law of thermodynamics: if system A is in thermal equilibrium with system C, and B is also in equilibrium with C, then A and B are in equilibrium with each other. This law defines temperature as the property that decides the direction of heat flow and lets a thermometer (C) compare two bodies.

Internal energy ($U$) is the total energy stored inside a system — the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of all its molecules. For an ideal gas it depends only on temperature, so $U$ rises when $T$ rises. Internal energy is a state function: its change $\Delta U$ depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path taken.

Heat ($\Delta Q$) is energy transferred because of a temperature difference, and work ($\Delta W$) is energy transferred by a force moving through a distance. Both are path-dependent (not state functions). When a gas expands by a small volume $dV$ against pressure $P$, the work done by the gas is $dW=P\,dV$, so over a finite change:

  • $W=\int_{V_1}^{V_2} P\,dV$ — equal to the area under the $P$–$V$ curve.
  • Work done by the gas (expansion) is positive; work done on the gas (compression) is negative.

The first law of thermodynamics is simply the law of conservation of energy applied to heat: the heat supplied to a system goes partly to raise its internal energy and partly to do external work:

  • $\Delta Q=\Delta U+\Delta W$.
  • Sign convention: $\Delta Q$ is positive when heat is added to the system; $\Delta W$ is positive when work is done by the system; $\Delta U$ is positive when the temperature rises.

The first law tells us energy cannot be created or destroyed, but it does not say in which direction a process will go — that is the job of the second law.

examples.problem: A gas absorbs 200 J of heat and does 80 J of work on its surroundings. Find the change in its internal energy.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Use the first law $\Delta Q=\Delta U+\Delta W$, so $\Delta U=\Delta Q-\Delta W$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute $\Delta Q=+200\ \text{J}$ (heat added) and $\Delta W=+80\ \text{J}$ (work by gas): $\Delta U=200-80$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $\Delta U=120\ \text{J}$.

Answer: $\Delta U=120\ \text{J}$ (internal energy increases).

examples.problem: 150 J of work is done on a gas while it releases 100 J of heat. Find the change in internal energy.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Apply $\Delta U=\Delta Q-\Delta W$ with correct signs.
  2. Step 2: Heat is released, so $\Delta Q=-100\ \text{J}$; work is done on the gas, so $\Delta W=-150\ \text{J}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $\Delta U=(-100)-(-150)=+50\ \text{J}$.

Answer: $\Delta U=+50\ \text{J}$ (internal energy increases).

examples.problem: A gas expands at a constant pressure of $2\times10^{5}\ \text{Pa}$ from a volume of $1\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$ to $3\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$. Find the work done by the gas.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: At constant pressure $W=P(V_2-V_1)$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $W=2\times10^{5}\times(3\times10^{-3}-1\times10^{-3})=2\times10^{5}\times2\times10^{-3}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $W=400\ \text{J}$.

Answer: $W=400\ \text{J}$ (done by the gas).

examples.problem: In a cyclic process a gas returns to its initial state. If it absorbs 500 J of heat during the cycle, how much net work does it do?
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: In a cyclic process the system returns to its starting state, so $\Delta U=0$ (internal energy is a state function).
  2. Step 2: From the first law $\Delta Q=\Delta U+\Delta W=0+\Delta W$.
  3. Step 3: Therefore $\Delta W=\Delta Q=500\ \text{J}$.

Answer: Net work done $=500\ \text{J}$.

examples.problem: When 1 g of water at 100 °C turns into steam it absorbs 2256 J of heat. The work done in expansion is 169 J. Find the increase in internal energy.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Use $\Delta U=\Delta Q-\Delta W$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute $\Delta Q=+2256\ \text{J}$ and $\Delta W=+169\ \text{J}$: $\Delta U=2256-169$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $\Delta U=2087\ \text{J}$.

Answer: $\Delta U=2087\ \text{J}$.

examples.problem: A system is taken from state A to state B by two paths. Along path 1, $\Delta Q=80\ \text{J}$ and $\Delta W=30\ \text{J}$. Along path 2 the work done is $10\ \text{J}$. Find the heat absorbed along path 2.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: $\Delta U$ depends only on the states A and B, so it is the same for both paths.
  2. Step 2: Path 1: $\Delta U=\Delta Q-\Delta W=80-30=50\ \text{J}$.
  3. Step 3: Path 2: $\Delta Q=\Delta U+\Delta W=50+10=60\ \text{J}$.

Answer: Heat absorbed along path 2 $=60\ \text{J}$.

recap: A thermodynamic system is described by state variables $P$, $V$, $T$, $n$ linked for an ideal gas by $PV=nRT$.
Zeroth law: bodies in thermal equilibrium with a third body are in equilibrium with each other — this defines temperature.
Internal energy $U$ is a state function; for an ideal gas it depends only on temperature.
Heat $\Delta Q$ and work $\Delta W$ are path-dependent; work done by a gas is $W=\int P\,dV$ = area under the $P$–$V$ curve.
First law: $\Delta Q=\Delta U+\Delta W$ — conservation of energy; $\Delta Q$ positive if heat added, $\Delta W$ positive if work done by the gas.

quiz.q: The first law of thermodynamics is a statement of the conservation of:
quiz.explanation: $\Delta Q=\Delta U+\Delta W$ is the law of conservation of energy applied to heat and work.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a state function?
quiz.explanation: Internal energy depends only on the state of the system; heat and work depend on the path.

quiz.q: The zeroth law of thermodynamics introduces the concept of:
quiz.explanation: The zeroth law establishes thermal equilibrium and thereby defines temperature.

quiz.q: The work done by a gas during expansion equals:
quiz.explanation: $W=\int P\,dV$, which is geometrically the area under the $P$–$V$ curve.

topics.title: Thermodynamic Processes
topics.concept:
A thermodynamic process is the way a system passes from one state to another. By holding one quantity fixed we obtain four important reversible processes, each with its own $P$–$V$ signature and its own form of the work done $W=\int P\,dV$.

1. Isothermal process (constant temperature). The gas is kept at a fixed temperature, usually by surrounding it with a heat reservoir and changing the volume slowly. Since $T$ is constant, for an ideal gas $\Delta U=0$, and the first law gives $\Delta Q=\Delta W$ — all the heat goes into work (or all the work removes heat).

  • It obeys Boyle's law $PV=\text{constant}$, so the $P$–$V$ curve is a hyperbola (isotherm).
  • Work done: $W=nRT\ln\!\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)=2.303\,nRT\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)$.

2. Adiabatic process (no heat exchange). The system is thermally insulated, so $\Delta Q=0$. The first law then gives $\Delta W=-\Delta U$ — the gas does work entirely at the cost of its internal energy, so an adiabatic expansion cools the gas and a compression heats it.

  • It obeys $PV^\gamma=\text{const}$ and $TV^{\gamma-1}=\text{const}$, where $\gamma=\frac{C_p}{C_v}$.
  • The adiabatic curve is steeper than the isotherm on a $P$–$V$ diagram.
  • Work done: $W=\frac{P_1V_1-P_2V_2}{\gamma-1}=\frac{nR(T_1-T_2)}{\gamma-1}$.

3. Isobaric process (constant pressure). The pressure is held fixed while the volume changes (e.g. a gas heated under a free piston).

  • Work done: $W=P(V_2-V_1)=nR(T_2-T_1)$.
  • Heat supplied: $\Delta Q=nC_p\,\Delta T$, using the molar specific heat at constant pressure.

4. Isochoric process (constant volume). The volume is fixed, so $dV=0$ and the gas does no work: $W=0$. All the heat raises the internal energy: $\Delta Q=\Delta U=nC_v\,\Delta T$.

Specific heats and Mayer's relation. A gas has two principal molar specific heats: $C_v$ (at constant volume) and $C_p$ (at constant pressure). Heating at constant pressure needs extra heat to do expansion work, so $C_p>C_v$. The first law applied to one mole gives Mayer's relation:

  • $C_p-C_v=R$ (with $R=8.314\ \text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$).
  • Their ratio is the adiabatic exponent $\gamma=\frac{C_p}{C_v}$: about $1.67$ for monatomic and $1.40$ for diatomic gases.

examples.problem: Two moles of an ideal gas expand isothermally at 300 K from a volume $V$ to $2V$. Find the work done. (Take $R=8.314\ \text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$.)
In an isothermal expansion a gas does 500 J of work. How much heat is absorbed by the gas?
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: For an isothermal process $T$ is constant, so $\Delta U=0$.
  2. Step 2: First law: $\Delta Q=\Delta U+\Delta W=0+\Delta W$.
  3. Step 3: Therefore $\Delta Q=\Delta W=500\ \text{J}$.

Answer: $\Delta Q=500\ \text{J}$ (all the absorbed heat becomes work).

examples.problem: The specific heat of a gas at constant volume is $C_v=20.8\ \text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$. Find $C_p$ and $\gamma$. (Take $R=8.314\ \text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$.)
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: By Mayer's relation $C_p=C_v+R$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $C_p=20.8+8.314=29.1\ \text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$.
  3. Step 3: $\gamma=\frac{C_p}{C_v}=\frac{29.1}{20.8}\approx1.40$ (a diatomic gas).

Answer: $C_p\approx29.1\ \text{J}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, $\gamma\approx1.40$.

examples.problem: A gas at $P_1=8\times10^{5}\ \text{Pa}$, $V_1=2\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$ expands adiabatically to $P_2=1\times10^{5}\ \text{Pa}$, $V_2=8\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$. Take $\gamma=1.4$. Find the work done by the gas.
A gas expands at a constant pressure of $1.5\times10^{5}\ \text{Pa}$ and absorbs 1200 J of heat. Its volume increases by $4\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$. Find the change in internal energy.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Isobaric work $W=P\,\Delta V=1.5\times10^{5}\times4\times10^{-3}=600\ \text{J}$.
  2. Step 2: First law: $\Delta U=\Delta Q-\Delta W=1200-600$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $\Delta U=600\ \text{J}$.

Answer: $\Delta U=600\ \text{J}$.

examples.problem: Air ($\gamma=1.4$) at $27\ ^\circ\text{C}$ is compressed adiabatically to one-eighth of its volume. Find the final temperature.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: For an adiabatic change $TV^{\gamma-1}=\text{const}$, so $T_2=T_1\left(\frac{V_1}{V_2}\right)^{\gamma-1}$.
  2. Step 2: $T_1=300\ \text{K}$, $\frac{V_1}{V_2}=8$, $\gamma-1=0.4$: $T_2=300\times8^{0.4}$.
  3. Step 3: $8^{0.4}=2.297$, so $T_2=300\times2.297\approx689\ \text{K}$.

Answer: $T_2\approx689\ \text{K}\;(\approx416\ ^\circ\text{C})$.

recap: Isothermal ($T$ const): $\Delta U=0$, $\Delta Q=\Delta W$, $PV=$ const, $W=nRT\ln\!\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)$.
Adiabatic ($\Delta Q=0$): $\Delta W=-\Delta U$, $PV^\gamma=$ const, $TV^{\gamma-1}=$ const, $W=\frac{P_1V_1-P_2V_2}{\gamma-1}$.
Isobaric ($P$ const): $W=P\,\Delta V=nR\,\Delta T$, heat $\Delta Q=nC_p\,\Delta T$.
Mayer's relation $C_p-C_v=R$ and $\gamma=\frac{C_p}{C_v}$ ($\approx1.67$ monatomic, $1.40$ diatomic); adiabatic curve is steeper than the isotherm.

quiz.q: In an isothermal process the change in internal energy of an ideal gas is:
quiz.explanation: Internal energy depends only on temperature; at constant $T$, $\Delta U=0$.

quiz.q: An adiabatic process obeys the relation:
In which process is the work done by the gas zero?
quiz.explanation: Isochoric means constant volume, so $dV=0$ and $W=\int P\,dV=0$.

quiz.q: Mayer's relation between the molar specific heats is:
quiz.explanation: Applying the first law to one mole at constant pressure gives $C_p-C_v=R$.

topics.title: Second Law, Heat Engines & Refrigerators
topics.concept:
The first law says energy is conserved, but it allows processes that never actually happen — heat flowing from a cold body to a hot one, or a single reservoir's heat being turned fully into work. The second law of thermodynamics rules these out by fixing the natural direction of thermal processes. It has two equivalent classic statements:

  • Kelvin–Planck statement: it is impossible to build an engine that, working in a cycle, takes heat from a single reservoir and converts all of it into work. Some heat must always be rejected.
  • Clausius statement: heat cannot flow on its own from a colder body to a hotter body; external work must be done to make this happen.

A heat engine is a device that converts heat into work in a repeating cycle. It absorbs heat $Q_1$ from a hot source (at $T_1$), converts part of it into useful work $W$, and rejects the remainder $Q_2$ to a cold sink (at $T_2$). By energy conservation $W=Q_1-Q_2$, and the efficiency is the fraction of input heat turned into work:

  • $\eta=\frac{W}{Q_1}=\frac{Q_1-Q_2}{Q_1}=1-\frac{Q_2}{Q_1}$.
  • Since $Q_2>0$ always (Kelvin–Planck), $\eta<1$: no engine can be 100% efficient.

The Carnot engine is an ideal, reversible engine and is the most efficient engine possible between two given temperatures. Its cycle has four reversible steps: isothermal expansion (heat $Q_1$ in at $T_1$), adiabatic expansion (cooling to $T_2$), isothermal compression (heat $Q_2$ out at $T_2$) and adiabatic compression (back to start). For the Carnot cycle the heat ratio equals the temperature ratio, so:

  • $\eta_{Carnot}=1-\frac{T_2}{T_1}$, with temperatures in kelvin.
  • Efficiency rises as the source gets hotter or the sink gets colder; $\eta=1$ only if $T_2=0\ \text{K}$, which is unattainable.

A refrigerator (or heat pump) is a heat engine run in reverse. Using external work $W$, it extracts heat $Q_2$ from a cold region (inside the fridge, at $T_2$) and dumps $Q_1=Q_2+W$ into the warmer room (at $T_1$). Its performance is measured by the coefficient of performance (COP), the heat removed per unit work:

  • $\beta=\frac{Q_2}{W}=\frac{Q_2}{Q_1-Q_2}$.
  • For an ideal (Carnot) refrigerator $\beta=\frac{T_2}{T_1-T_2}$.
  • Unlike efficiency, the COP can be greater than 1 — that is why a refrigerator can move more heat than the work it consumes.

examples.problem: A Carnot engine works between a source at 500 K and a sink at 300 K. Find its efficiency.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Use $\eta=1-\frac{T_2}{T_1}$ with temperatures in kelvin.
  2. Step 2: Substitute: $\eta=1-\frac{300}{500}=1-0.6$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $\eta=0.4=40\%$.

Answer: $\eta=40\%$.

examples.problem: A heat engine absorbs 1000 J from a source and rejects 700 J to the sink in each cycle. Find the work done and the efficiency.
A Carnot engine has an efficiency of 50% when the sink is at 300 K. Find the temperature of the source.
A refrigerator extracts 240 J of heat from its interior while consuming 60 J of electrical work in each cycle. Find its coefficient of performance and the heat rejected to the room.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: COP $\beta=\frac{Q_2}{W}=\frac{240}{60}=4$.
  2. Step 2: Heat rejected $Q_1=Q_2+W=240+60$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $Q_1=300\ \text{J}$.

Answer: $\beta=4$; heat rejected $Q_1=300\ \text{J}$.

examples.problem: An ideal refrigerator maintains its interior at 250 K while the room is at 300 K. Find its coefficient of performance.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: For an ideal (Carnot) refrigerator $\beta=\frac{T_2}{T_1-T_2}$.
  2. Step 2: Substitute $T_2=250\ \text{K}$, $T_1=300\ \text{K}$: $\beta=\frac{250}{300-250}=\frac{250}{50}$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $\beta=5$.

Answer: $\beta=5$.

examples.problem: A Carnot engine takes 2000 J of heat from a source at 400 K and rejects heat to a sink at 300 K. Find the work done per cycle.
examples.solution:
1. Step 1: Carnot efficiency $\eta=1-\frac{T_2}{T_1}=1-\frac{300}{400}=0.25$.
  2. Step 2: Work done $W=\eta\,Q_1=0.25\times2000$.
  3. Step 3: Compute: $W=500\ \text{J}$ (and rejected heat $Q_2=Q_1-W=1500\ \text{J}$).

Answer: $W=500\ \text{J}$.

recap: Second law fixes the direction of heat flow: Kelvin–Planck (no engine fully converts heat from one reservoir to work) and Clausius (heat does not flow cold→hot by itself).
Heat engine: absorbs $Q_1$, rejects $Q_2$, does work $W=Q_1-Q_2$; efficiency $\eta=1-\frac{Q_2}{Q_1}<1$.
Carnot engine is the most efficient reversible engine: $\eta=1-\frac{T_2}{T_1}$ (temperatures in kelvin).
Carnot efficiency rises with a hotter source or colder sink; $\eta=1$ only if $T_2=0\ \text{K}$, which is unattainable.
Refrigerator (engine in reverse): COP $\beta=\frac{Q_2}{W}=\frac{Q_2}{Q_1-Q_2}$; ideal $\beta=\frac{T_2}{T_1-T_2}$, which can exceed 1.

quiz.q: The Kelvin–Planck statement of the second law says it is impossible to:
options: convert all heat from a single reservoir into work in a cycle
quiz.explanation: An engine working in a cycle must reject some heat; it cannot turn all the heat from one reservoir into work.

quiz.q: The efficiency of a Carnot engine working between $T_1$ and $T_2$ is:
The efficiency of any heat engine is always:
quiz.explanation: Because some heat $Q_2>0$ is always rejected, $\eta=1-\frac{Q_2}{Q_1}<1$.

quiz.q: The coefficient of performance of an ideal refrigerator is:
quiz.explanation: For an ideal refrigerator $\beta=\frac{Q_2}{W}=\frac{T_2}{T_1-T_2}$, which can be greater than 1.

questions.q: The first law of thermodynamics is expressed as:
questions.explanation: Heat added equals the rise in internal energy plus the work done by the gas: $\Delta Q=\Delta U+\Delta W$.

questions.q: The zeroth law of thermodynamics defines the concept of:
questions.explanation: Thermal equilibrium between bodies via a third defines temperature.

questions.q: For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on:
questions.explanation: Internal energy of an ideal gas is a function of temperature alone.

questions.q: The work done by a gas is given by:
questions.explanation: $W=\int P\,dV$, the area under the $P$–$V$ curve.

questions.q: In an isothermal process for an ideal gas, $\Delta U$ equals:
An adiabatic process obeys:
The work done in an isochoric process is:
Mayer's relation is:
questions.explanation: $C_p-C_v=R$ for one mole of an ideal gas.

questions.q: The work done in an isothermal expansion from $V_1$ to $V_2$ is:
The efficiency of a Carnot engine between source $T_1$ and sink $T_2$ is:
A heat engine takes 1000 J and rejects 750 J per cycle. Its efficiency is:
The efficiency of any heat engine is always:
questions.explanation: Some heat is always rejected, so $\eta=1-\frac{Q_2}{Q_1}<1$.

questions.q: For a Carnot engine the efficiency is 100% only if:
A Carnot engine works between 400 K and 300 K. Its efficiency is:
The coefficient of performance of a refrigerator is:
In a cyclic process the change in internal energy is:
questions.explanation: After a full cycle the system returns to its initial state, so $\Delta U=0$.

questions.explanation: $W=0$ at constant volume, so $\Delta Q=\Delta U=nC_v\Delta T$.

questions.q: On a $P$–$V$ diagram, the adiabatic curve compared with the isotherm through the same point is:
questions.explanation: Adiabatic slope is $\gamma$ times the isothermal slope, and $\gamma>1$, so it is steeper.

questions.q: A gas does 50 J of work in an isothermal expansion and 40 J in an adiabatic expansion between the same volumes. In the adiabatic case the internal energy change is:
A monatomic gas ($\gamma=5/3$) is compressed adiabatically to one-eighth of its volume. The temperature becomes (from $T$):
The slope of the adiabatic curve to the isothermal curve at a point is in the ratio:
questions.explanation: Adiabatic slope $=\gamma P/V$, isothermal slope $=P/V$, ratio $\gamma:1$.

In a cyclic process the area enclosed by the loop on a $P$–$V$ diagram represents:
options: the net heat absorbed and net work done
questions.explanation: For a cycle $\Delta U=0$, so net heat = net work = area of the loop.

It is impossible to convert heat completely into work in a cyclic process. This is a statement of:
questions.explanation: This is the Kelvin–Planck form of the second law of thermodynamics.
